मौसम विभाग के अनुसार न्यूनतम तापमान में भी गिरावट आ सकती है। गुरुवार को न्यूनतम तापमान 20 डिग्री पर बना रहने की संभावना है।

जागरण संवाददाता, देहरादून। उत्तराखंड में करवाचौथ पर मौसम का मिजाज बदल गया। गंगोत्री धाम केदारनाथ और बदरीनाथ में बर्फबारी हुई है। जिससे धाम में मौसम काफी ठंडा हो गया है। राज्य के कई इलाकों में बादल छाए रहे। वहीं ऋषिकेश, पौड़ी, श्रीनगर और कोटद्वार में बारिश हुई।
मौसम विभाग ने गुरुवार को आंशिक बादलों के बीच प्रदेश के दस जिलों में गर्जन, आकाशीय बिजली चमकने और तेज झोंकेदार हवाएं चलने की चेतावनी जारी की थी। वहीं, शुक्रवार को प्रदेश के अधिकतर क्षेत्रों में तेज वर्षा होने की संभावना जताई गई थी। इससे तापमान में गिरावट आने और मौसम में ठंडक बढ़ने के आसार हैं।

पिछले कुछ दिनों से प्रदेश में मौसम शुष्क बना हुआ है। मैदानी क्षेत्रों में तेज धूप खिलने से दिन के तापमान में वृद्धि हुई है, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य बना हुआ है। इसके चलते दिन और रात के तापमान में अंतर बढ़ गया है। हालांकि, चक्रवाती तूफान अर्नब और पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के असर के बीच मौसम का मिजाज बदलने के आसार हैं।

राज्य के शेष जिलों में कहीं-कहीं बहुत हल्की से हल्की वर्षा के आसार हैं। ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में 3500 मीटर या उससे अधिक ऊंचाई पर बर्फबारी भी हो सकती है।

दिल्ली-एनसीआर में आज से बदलेगा मौसम: दो दिन बारिश, ओलावृष्टि और तेज हवा के आसार, जानिए कितना गिर सकता है पारा
दिल्ली-एनसीआर में बृहस्पतिवार से मौसम का मिजाज बदलेगा। अगले दो दिन हल्की बारिश, ओलावृष्टि होगी। 30 से 40 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चलेंगी।
विस्तार
दिल्ली-एनसीआर में मौसम का मिजाज बृहस्पतिवार से बदलने जा रहा है। अगले दो दिन तक आसमान में बादल छाए रहने के साथ हल्की बारिश के आसार हैं। इस दौरान 30 से 40 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं। कुछ स्थानों पर ओलावृष्टि भी हो सकती है। इस सबका मिला-जुला असर तापमान में गिरावट के तौर पर दिखेगा। आईएमडी के मुताबिक, इसकी वजह बंगाल की खाड़ी में सक्रिय चक्रवाती तूफान ‘अर्नब’ और उत्तर भारत का पश्चिमी विक्षाेभ बन रहा है। इससे दो दिनों तक दिल्ली-एनसीआर मौसमी दशाओं के तेज बदलाव के दौर से गुजरेगा।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 29 अक्तूबर की सुबह और दोपहर के दौरान हल्की बारिश के एक से अधिक दौर आने की संभावना है। कई स्थानों पर बिजली कड़कने और 30 से 40 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चल सकती हैं। कुछ जगहों पर मध्यम बारिश भी हो सकती है। इस दिन अधिकतम तापमान 26 से 28 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 16 से 18 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहने का अनुमान है। अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से तीन से पांच डिग्री तक नीचे रह सकता है। इससे दिन में मौसम अपेक्षाकृत ठंडा महसूस होगा।

अगले दिन शुक्रवार को भी मौसम में बदलाव नहीं आएगा। आसमान में आंशिक से लेकर आमतौर पर बादल छाए रह सकते हैं। सुबह से दोपहर बाद तक हल्की बारिश के साथ गरज-चमक और तेज हवाएं चलने की संभावना है। इस दिन अधिकतम तापमान 27 से 29 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 17 से 19 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रह सकता है। अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से एक से तीन डिग्री कम रहने का अनुमान है। हालांकि, न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य से ऊपर रह सकता है। दोपहर में हवा की गति 25 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे तक पहुंच सकती है।
बुधवार सामान्य से ज्यादा रहा अधिकतम तापमान
मौसम विभाग के मुताबिक, बुधवार दिल्ली का अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से 0.8 डिग्री ऊपर 31.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। वहीं, न्यूनतम तापमान सामान्य से 0.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस कम रहा। अगले दो दिनों तक इसमें तीन से पांच डिग्री सेल्सियस की कमी आने का अनुमान है। इससे दिल्लीवालों का सर्द मौसम का अहसास होगा।

संवाद न्यूज एजेंसी, चरखी दादरी
विज्ञापन
चरखी दादरी। जिले में बदलते मौसम का असर लोगों के स्वास्थ्य पर दिखाई देने लगा है। सुबह-शाम ठंड और दिन में गर्मी के कारण खांसी, जुकाम और वायरल बुखार के मरीजों की संख्या बढ़ रही है। सरकारी अस्पताल में ओपीडी का आंकड़ा 1200 के पार पहुंच गया है। चिकित्सकों के अनुसार पिछले दिनों की तुलना में खांसी, जुकाम और वायरल बुखार से पीड़ित मरीजों में करीब 30 प्रतिशत तक बढ़ोतरी हुई है। वहीं वायु गुणवत्ता सूचकांक 151 के पार पहुंचने से भी सांस संबंधी परेशानी से जूझ रहे लोगों को सतर्क रहने की जरूरत है।
दिन-रात के तापमान में अंतर से बढ़ रही परेशानी
मौसम में लगातार बदलाव के कारण दिन और रात के तापमान में काफी अंतर बना हुआ है। दिन का अधिकतम तापमान करीब 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच रहा है जबकि रात का न्यूनतम तापमान करीब 17 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया जा रहा है। दोनों के तापमान में लगभग 14 डिग्री का अंतर होने से सुबह और शाम के समय ठंड महसूस होती है जबकि दोपहर में गर्मी रहती है। ऐसे में लोग मौसम के अनुसार कपड़े नहीं पहन पाते और सर्दी-जुकाम जैसी समस्याओं की चपेट में आ जाते हैं।
बच्चों और बुजुर्गों को अधिक सावधानी बरतने की जरूरत
चिकित्सकों के अनुसार मौसम में बदलाव के दौरान बच्चों, बुजुर्गों और पहले से बीमार लोगों को विशेष सावधानी बरतनी चाहिए। खांसी, जुकाम, गले में खराश, बुखार और शरीर में दर्द जैसी शिकायत होने पर लापरवाही नहीं करनी चाहिए। वायरल संक्रमण के लक्षण दिखाई देने पर चिकित्सक से परामर्श लेना चाहिए। साथ ही, बिना चिकित्सकीय सलाह के दवाइयां लेने से बचना चाहिए।
विज्ञापन
एक्यूआई 151 के पार
जिले में वायु गुणवत्ता सूचकांक 151 के पार पहुंच गया है। वायु प्रदूषण और बदलते मौसम का असर सांस संबंधी बीमारियों से पीड़ित लोगों पर अधिक पड़ सकता है। ऐसे लोगों को धूल-धुएं के संपर्क में आने से बचना चाहिए। सुबह-शाम बाहर निकलते समय मौसम का ध्यान रखें और परेशानी बढ़ने पर चिकित्सकीय सलाह लें।
बचाव के लिए अपनाएं ये सावधानियां
चिकित्सकों के अनुसार बदलते मौसम में पर्याप्त पानी पीना, संतुलित आहार लेना और साफ-सफाई का ध्यान रखना जरूरी है। ठंडे और गर्म वातावरण में अचानक बदलाव से बचना चाहिए। खांसते या छींकते समय मुंह और नाक को ढकें तथा हाथों की नियमित सफाई करें। बुखार या संक्रमण के लक्षण लंबे समय तक बने रहने पर जांच करवाएं। सावधानी बरतकर मौसमी बीमारियों से बचाव किया जा सकता है।
वर्सन:
बदलते हुए माैसम से लोग बीमार पड़ रहे हैं ऐसे में लोगों को विशेष सावधानियां रखने की जरूरत है। ज्यादा दिक्कत होते ही तुरंत चिकित्सक से संपर्क करें। - डॉ. राहुल अरोड़ा, प्रवक्ता, स्वास्थ्य विभाग।

Heat illness insurance payouts surge fourfold in Gyeonggi’s record summer
Gyeonggi’s climate insurance program paid far more heat-related claims in six months than during the previous full year as extreme weather intensified.
Heat shimmers rise from a road in Yeongdeungpo District, western Seoul, on Aug. 4 as the highest-level heat wave emergency warning remains in effect.YONHAP
Payouts for heat-related illnesses under Gyeonggi's climate insurance program more than quadrupled in just six months compared to the previous full-year period, as record-breaking heat waves took a growing toll on residents' health this summer.
The number of claims also more than doubled, and the insurer paid out a newly introduced death benefit in four cases. With extreme weather increasingly threatening people's health and livelihoods, demand for insurance against climate-related damage is likely to grow.
Payouts for heat-related illness diagnoses and daily hospitalization benefits under Gyeonggi's climate insurance program totaled 208.64 million won ($157,000) across 2,856 claims between April 11 and Oct. 15, according to insurance industry sources on Oct. 25.
That was approximately 4.2 times the 50.26 million won paid out during the previous full-year coverage period, from April 11 last year to April 10 this year. The number of claims also rose about 2.3 times from 1,264.
In other words, payouts over roughly six months far exceeded those made during the entire previous insurance period.
Including newly introduced benefits for emergency room visits and deaths, total payouts reached 233.94 million won across 2,992 claims.
This year, Gyeonggi introduced a 3 million won death benefit for people who die from heat- or cold-related illnesses or climate-related disasters. The city paid four claims totaling 12 million won in September and October.
An estimated 36 people died from heat-related illnesses nationwide this summer, including three reported deaths in Gyeonggi, according to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency. All three deaths in Gyeonggi are believed to have qualified for the new death benefit.
As extreme heat took a particularly heavy toll on older adults and other vulnerable groups, the newly introduced emergency room benefit also recorded 132 claims totaling 13.3 million won.
Climate insurance covers illnesses, accidents and income losses caused by extreme weather events such as heat waves, cold spells and torrential rain. Gyeonggi operates the program as a group insurance policy and pays the full premiums on behalf of its residents, who are automatically enrolled without having to apply.
When a regional government purchases climate insurance for its residents, eligible individuals can file claims for heat-related or cold-related illnesses or climate-related accidents that meet the policy's coverage requirements. They must submit supporting documents, and the insurer pays benefits after reviewing the claims. Residents do not need to purchase individual policies.
Jeju Island also introduced climate insurance in July this year, though its program takes a different approach. While Gyeonggi focuses on covering health-related damage, Jeju's program aims to compensate workers for income lost when extreme heat forces them to stop working.
Launched on July 28, the program covers eligible day laborers at public construction sites. If a heat wave warning or similar alert is issued before 1 p.m. and work is suspended, workers can receive partial compensation for income lost during the suspension.
Private insurers are also expanding their climate-related offerings.
Tongyang Life Insurance launched a small-scale insurance product in August that covers heat-related and cold-related illnesses.
KB Insurance introduced weather-related damage insurance for traditional markets, available through merchants' associations, and added optional coverage for heat-related and cold-related illnesses to its travel insurance products.
NongHyup Property & Casualty Insurance offers additional coverage for livestock losses caused by extreme heat.
As concerns about extreme weather damage grow, insurance payouts could rise further.
Claims can be filed up to three years after an incident, so benefits for illnesses that occurred during the coverage period may be paid later. The payout for a heat-related illness diagnosis also increased from 100,000 won to 150,000 won this year, while growing awareness of the program could encourage more residents to file claims.
"We are receiving about 150 to 200 inquiries and claims a day," an official at the insurer underwriting Gyeonggi's climate insurance program said.
However, critics point to the program's heavy concentration of payouts on transportation expenses for medical visits among climate-vulnerable residents as a persistent limitation.
The program provides 20,000 won per medical visit for transportation costs, up to five times per eligible resident.
Of the 39,451 claims paid under Gyeonggi's climate insurance program this year, 36,301, or 92 percent, were for transportation expenses. That was down 2.6 percentage points from 94.6 percent last year, but transportation expenses still accounted for more than nine out of every 10 claims, raising questions about whether the program provides sufficient protection against the direct health and financial consequences of climate-related illnesses and accidents.

Researchers have built a garment that ventilates itself, opening small fabric flaps wherever sweat accumulates, without batteries, fans, or pumps. The system, described in the open-access journal Fashion and Textiles, relies on a composite textile that curls open in response to moisture, and a sweating thermal manikin test showed that the resulting ventilated garment improved localized evaporative heat release in several high-sweat body regions. The work was led by Hyeon-seon Cho, Soah Park, Hyukjoo Yang, Seungsin Lee, and Sumin Koo, and was published on 30 September 2026.
The core of the design is a bilayer moisture-responsive fabric modeled on hygromorphic structures found in nature, such as pinecones, which open and close as humidity fluctuates. In engineered bilayer actuators, a hydrophilic layer swells when it absorbs moisture while a hydrophobic outer layer resists that deformation, generating internal stress gradients that force the material to bend or curl. The team laminated two commercially available hydrophilic cotton fabrics, a plain-woven cotton designated CW and a single jersey knit designated CK, with a hydrophobic polyurethane nanofiber web, or PUN, produced by electrospinning from pure polyurethane. The nanoweb had a density of 19.72 grams per square meter and a thickness of 0.064 millimeters, and the layers were bonded with a roller laminating machine that heat-pressed the pre-attached stacks at 100 degrees Celsius at a processing speed of roughly 900 millimeters per minute.
Six composite fabrics were fabricated by applying one, two, or three layers of PUN to each of the two cotton substrates. Physical characterization showed that increasing the number of nanoweb layers gradually increased both thickness and weight. Among single-layer specimens, CW/PUN1 measured 0.24 millimeters thick and weighed 0.0438 grams, while CK/PUN1 was thicker at 0.33 millimeters but lighter at 0.0379 grams. Three-layer versions reached 0.33 millimeters for CW/PUN3 and 0.36 millimeters for CK/PUN3, with corresponding weights of 0.0599 and 0.0478 grams. Scanning electron microscopy confirmed that the electrospun nanofibers retained their straight, undamaged morphology after lamination, formed continuous hydrophobic zones across the fabric surface, and adhered strongly to the substrates with no evidence of delamination.
To quantify moisture responsiveness, the researchers floated rectangular specimens, measuring 2.5 by 1.3 centimeters, on distilled water in a Petri dish with the hydrophilic side facing downward. Surface tension kept the fabrics from sinking, and a camera recorded the spontaneous curling over ten minutes. Computer vision algorithms based on OpenCV converted the observed curvature from pixels to centimeters, using a conversion factor derived from the known specimen length. The results showed a clear trend: curling increased as more PUN layers were added, because the thicker hydrophobic outer web amplified the swelling mismatch between the layers. Curvature radii fell from 0.37 centimeters for CW/PUN1 to 0.28 centimeters for CW/PUN3, and from 0.22 centimeters for CK/PUN1 to 0.16 centimeters for CK/PUN3, with smaller radii indicating stronger deformation.
The knitted composites consistently outperformed their woven counterparts. The researchers attribute this to the looped structure of the knit, which offers higher porosity and greater flexibility than the woven structure, allowing moisture to diffuse more readily and allowing localized swelling to translate into global curl-up deformation. The knit’s loops also compressed more during lamination, which explains why CK-based specimens gained less thickness than CW-based ones as layers were added. On the strength of these results, CK/PUN3, with the smallest curvature radius and therefore the strongest moisture response, was selected as the functional fabric for the garment.
The ventilated garment was designed as a long-sleeve hoodie, a choice informed by earlier findings that agricultural workers favor long sleeves and head coverage during summer fieldwork. The base garment was made from a stretchable knit of 87 percent polyester and 13 percent polyurethane, weighing 246.85 grams, and was first visualized in CLO 3D software before being physically prototyped. Ten uniformly sized CK/PUN3 flaps were integrated into regions of high sweat production identified from published human sweat distribution data: three flaps in the bra triangle area of the front torso and seven across the upper back. Mesh panels of 100 percent polyester were added along the center of the hood and the underarm areas to further improve airflow. The flaps are designed to open when exposed to moisture, enhancing ventilation precisely where the wearer sweats most.
Performance was evaluated on a sweating thermal manikin with 20 independently controlled segments, following the ASTM F2370 protocol in a climate-controlled chamber set to 35 degrees Celsius with 40 percent relative humidity and air velocity below 0.3 meters per second. Distilled water was supplied to each segment at 1000 milliliters per square meter per hour to simulate a fully soaked skin surface, and each garment condition was tested in duplicate. Compared with an unmodified control garment, the ventilated garment reduced intrinsic evaporative resistance by 7.50 percent, from 6.93 to 6.41 square meters pascals per watt, and total evaporative resistance by 2.17 percent, from 24.00 to 23.48 square meters pascals per watt.
Regional heat flux measurements across nine body regions revealed more pronounced localized gains. Heat flux rose by 26.78 percent in the abdominal region, from 65.54 to 83.09 watts per square meter, and by 18.59 percent in the chest, reaching 153.77 watts per square meter, both areas covered by the moisture-responsive flaps. The head region showed a 7.68 percent increase, to 223.31 watts per square meter, which the authors attribute to the mesh panel in the hood. The back, where the flaps were applied directly, showed only a 4.14 percent increase, possibly because close contact between the garment and the manikin restricted air movement. Heat flux was higher for the ventilated garment in every region tested except the right upper arm.
The authors are careful to frame these results as preliminary laboratory evidence rather than proof of real-world performance. The manikin was static, so the tests did not capture human thermoregulatory responses, body movement, or the effects of motion on flap opening, garment displacement, and air exchange. No human wear trials were conducted, meaning subjective comfort, perceived ventilation, fit, and mobility could not be assessed. The duplicate testing also limits statistical reliability, and the study covered only an upper-body garment with specific ventilation zones. Durability questions, including washing stability and long-term performance after repeated moisture-response cycles, remain unexamined, and the authors call for future studies addressing these gaps along with wearer trials under varied temperature, humidity, and activity conditions.
Even so, the study demonstrates a passive, energy-free alternative to existing personal cooling systems. Air-cooled, liquid-cooled, and phase-change garments typically depend on external power, added components, or added weight, which limits their practicality for outdoor workers in agriculture and construction who face prolonged heat exposure and risks including heat stroke, dehydration, and reduced work efficiency. The ventilated garment’s value, the authors argue, lies not in a large whole-garment reduction in evaporative resistance but in a low-burden, supplementary ventilation strategy that targets localized heat release in high-sweat regions while maintaining the coverage of long-sleeved workwear. Future work is planned to extend the responsive design to other body regions, evaluate long-term usability through participant-based trials, and investigate performance changes after repeated use and washing.

Cumulative exposure to heatwaves is associated with an increased risk of following the most vulnerable trajectory of intrinsic capacity among middle-aged and older adults in China, according to a study published in BMC Public Health that analyzed data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Intrinsic capacity, a multidimensional construct proposed by the World Health Organization as a core indicator of healthy aging, spans five domains: locomotion, sensory function, vitality, psychological well-being, and cognition.
The researchers drew on 1,393 participants aged 45 to 80 years who had complete intrinsic capacity assessments across three waves of CHARLS, in 2011, 2013, and 2015. Intrinsic capacity was operationalized as a composite score ranging from 0 to 10 across the five domains. K-means clustering was used to identify heterogeneous trajectories of capacity over time, and extreme temperature events were defined using city-specific daily apparent temperature, with a heatwave defined as temperature at or above the 95th percentile for at least three days and a cold spell as temperature at or below the 5th percentile for at least three days.
Three distinct trajectories emerged from the clustering analysis: a high-stable group comprising 41.3 percent of participants, a moderate-declining group comprising 26.4 percent, and a low-declining group comprising 32.3 percent. Using multinomial logistic regression with progressive adjustment for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and health-related covariates, the team examined whether cumulative heatwave days between 2011 and 2015 were associated with membership in these trajectory groups.
Each additional heatwave day significantly increased the risk of belonging to the low-declining trajectory, with a fully adjusted relative risk ratio of 1.035 (95 percent confidence interval: 1.012 to 1.058; P = 0.003). The association was more pronounced among participants with primary school education or below, who had a relative risk ratio of 1.07 (95 percent confidence interval: 1.04 to 1.11), and among rural residents, who had a relative risk ratio of 1.05 (95 percent confidence interval: 1.03 to 1.08). Significant effect modification was observed for both education (P for interaction = 0.031) and residence (P for interaction = 0.024), indicating that the association differed across these socioeconomic subgroups.
In contrast, cold spell days showed no significant association with trajectory membership, with a relative risk ratio of 1.02 (95 percent confidence interval: 0.96 to 1.08; P = 0.554). The authors report that sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the results.
The study is observational in design, and its findings describe associations between cumulative heatwave exposure and trajectory membership rather than established causal effects. The analysis was limited to participants with complete intrinsic capacity assessments across the three CHARLS waves, and the exposure window covered the 2011 to 2015 period in China. The authors note that global climate change has increased the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme temperature events while population aging poses growing public health challenges, and that the association between extreme temperature events and longitudinal intrinsic capacity trajectories had remained unknown prior to this work.
The authors conclude that cumulative heatwave exposure is associated with an increased risk of belonging to the most vulnerable intrinsic capacity trajectory among Chinese middle-aged and older adults, particularly among socioeconomically disadvantaged groups, and that these findings underscore the need for targeted climate adaptation strategies to protect functional health in aging populations.

Heatwave Festival
Heatwave Festival has announced its return to Port Douglas, running from Friday to Sunday, February 12 to 14 on the back of the first event which injected an estimated $350,000 into town in the low season.
Organisers Andrew Dalbertanson and Kent Fordham report that Heatwave 2026 brought more than 850 guests into town for the festival and their visitor-spending estimate covers a four-day visit period encompassing accommodation, hospitality and purchases from local businesses.

The opportunity extends to other parts of the tourism industry. Airport transfers and local transport connect visitors with the destination, while shops, reef experiences and rainforest tours offer reasons to explore between events or extend a stay.

October can bring cooler mornings, but afternoons in many parts of India can still feel uncomfortably hot. As the season changes, people may stop carrying water bottles, skip sunscreen or return to intense outdoor workouts. These changes seem harmless, but the body responds to actual weather conditions, not the calendar.
Drinking water only when thirst strikes
When the heat feels less intense, drinking enough water can slip down the priority list. Long commutes, office meetings and daily errands can make people overlook their fluid needs, even when they continue to sweat.
Dehydration can cause headaches, tiredness, dizziness and difficulty concentrating. Carrying a water bottle and drinking regularly throughout the day can help. Older adults, children and outdoor workers need particular attention. Those advised to restrict fluids for medical reasons should follow their doctor's guidance.
Assuming sunscreen is no longer necessary
Sunscreen often disappears from daily routines once summer seems over. However, ultraviolet (UV) radiation can damage the skin throughout the year, even when the weather feels comfortable.
The US Food and Drug Administration explains how to protect yourself from UV radiation.
Broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, protective clothing, hats and shade can help reduce exposure. Sunscreen should be reapplied according to the product instructions.
Dressing for the season instead of the temperature
A pleasant morning can turn into a hot afternoon, especially during a long commute or an outdoor work shift. Heavy, tight clothing may trap heat and make sweat evaporation less effective.
Lightweight, breathable fabrics can improve comfort. As Dr Ajay Sawant, Consultant – Internal Medicine, KIMS Hospital, Thane, explained, “People should respond to the conditions they are experiencing rather than assuming that the risk of heat-related illness ends with summer.”
That advice applies to everyday clothing choices, too. Dressing according to the day's actual conditions can make prolonged outdoor exposure more manageable.
Returning to intense workouts too quickly
When the weather seems more comfortable, it is tempting to increase running distances, resume outdoor sports or exercise harder. But heat and humidity can still put extra strain on the body.
Choose cooler hours where possible, increase exercise intensity gradually and take regular breaks. Stop exercising if unusual weakness, nausea, headache or dizziness develops. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's heat and health guidance offers advice on preventing heat-related illness.
Brushing off early signs of heat stress
Feeling unusually drained after an ordinary walk may seem harmless, but persistent symptoms deserve attention. Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea and dizziness can indicate heat exhaustion. Move to a cooler place, stop physical activity and begin cooling the body.
Dr Sawant stresses that “Regular hydration, appropriate sun protection and recognising early symptoms of heat stress remain important whenever temperatures stay high.”
Confusion, seizures, fainting or a very high body temperature can indicate heatstroke, a medical emergency. Call emergency services immediately rather than waiting for home remedies to work.
October may signal a seasonal change, but it does not guarantee relief from heat. Keeping daily routines flexible and paying attention to the body's warning signs can help protect health until temperatures genuinely fall.

Forensic scientists trying to pin down the time of death rely on biochemical and tissue changes that unfold after the heart stops, but those changes are never purely a product of death itself. They are shaped by what a body lived through before it died, and the new study examined whether one such premortem condition, heat stroke, alters postmortem biochemical and histological changes. A new experimental study in rats, published in the Egyptian Journal of Forensic Sciences, reports that heat stroke leaves a measurable imprint on postmortem liver enzyme levels and tissue decay, and that pretreating animals with omega-3 fatty acids significantly altered one of those biochemical signatures without meaningfully changing another.
The research team, led by Radwa B. Hassan and colleagues, set out to answer a question with direct medicolegal consequences: if a person dies during or after severe hyperthermia, do the usual postmortem markers behave the way forensic textbooks expect? The motivation is timely. As global warming increases the frequency and severity of heatwaves, deaths linked to heat-related illness are expected to rise, and ambient temperature is already known to be among the most powerful modifiers of autolysis, microbial activity, and tissue decomposition. Traditional indicators of the postmortem interval, such as body cooling, hypostasis, and rigor mortis, are considered reliable mainly within the first 48 to 72 hours, after which their accuracy declines sharply. Anything that systematically shifts the biochemical and histological timeline in heat-exposed bodies could complicate interval estimates in exactly the situations where they matter most.
To test this, the investigators ran a controlled, prospective, randomized, interventional animal study involving 40 healthy adult male albino rats aged 3 to 4 months and weighing 170 to 200 grams. Animals with prior illness, dermatological abnormalities, or abnormal baseline liver enzymes were excluded. The rats were randomly assigned to four groups of ten each: a control group, an omega-3-only group, a heat-stroke group, and an omega-3-pretreated heat-stroke group. After 14 days of quarantine and acclimatization, treated animals received oral omega-3 at 400 milligrams per kilogram daily for 28 days, delivered through a dedicated oropharyngeal tube for each rat. Heat stroke was simulated by placing anesthetized rats in a controlled environmental chamber at 39.5 plus or minus 0.5 degrees Celsius for 180 minutes, with rectal core temperature continuously monitored. Animals were anesthetized with intraperitoneal sodium pentobarbital before heat exposure and euthanized according to ethical guidelines.
The biochemical core of the study focused on two familiar enzymes. Alanine aminotransferase, or ALT, sits predominantly in the hepatocyte cytoplasm and is relatively liver-specific, while aspartate aminotransferase, or AST, occurs in both cytoplasm and mitochondria and is abundant in liver, skeletal muscle, and erythrocytes. Both leak into the circulation when hepatocellular injury disrupts cell membranes, and both can continue rising after death as autolysis releases intracellular contents. Blood was drawn after euthanasia and samples were stored alongside the carcasses under the same experimental conditions, then analyzed at predetermined postmortem intervals of 0, 12, 24, 36, and 48 hours using a Beckman UniCel DxC800 Synchron system. Liver and skin samples were collected at intervals stretching from 0 to 168 hours, fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 5 to 6 micrometers, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin for blinded qualitative assessment by two independent observers, with disagreements resolved by a third.
The statistical results split cleanly down the middle. ALT and AST both increased progressively with advancing postmortem interval in every group, with p values below 0.001, confirming that these enzymes behave in a strongly time-dependent fashion after death. Heat-exposed rats showed significantly higher levels of both enzymes than control and omega-3-only animals. But the decisive finding came from a two-by-two factorial analysis treating heat stroke and omega-3 pretreatment as separate factors. For ALT, the Heat Stroke by Omega-3 interaction was highly significant, with an F value of 55.947 and p below 0.001, meaning the effect of omega-3 depended on whether the animal had experienced heat stroke.
AST told a different story. Although AST also climbed significantly over time and heat stroke produced a significant main effect, the Heat Stroke by Omega-3 interaction was not statistically significant (F = 0.765, p = 0.388). AST levels were numerically lower in the omega-3-pretreated heat-stroke group, but the differences from the heat-stroke group alone were not significant at any individual postmortem interval or overall (p = 0.162). The authors attribute this asymmetry partly to the biology of the two enzymes: ALT has a longer circulating half-life, roughly 40 to 60 hours in rats and comparable species, versus approximately 12 hours for AST, and AST is far more vulnerable to confounding from hemolysis and muscle injury because of its high erythrocyte content. ALT may therefore be the more informative marker for detecting acute and subacute hepatocellular injury in this setting.
The histological findings reinforced the biochemical picture, with an important caveat. In the heat-exposed groups, liver sections at the moment of death already showed distorted hepatic cords, severe congestion of blood sinusoids, cytoplasmic vacuolization, hydropic changes, focal fatty changes, and inflammatory infiltration. Autolysis then progressed faster in heat-exposed animals regardless of treatment: control and omega-3-only rats retained recognizable hepatic architecture up to about 72 hours postmortem, whereas heat-exposed groups showed disrupted organization and fragmented hepatic cords as early as 48 hours, and complete loss of recognizable architecture by 120 hours, at which point sampling stopped. In the omega-3-pretreated heat-stroke group, congestion, hemorrhage, and structural damage appeared less pronounced at corresponding intervals, with better-preserved hepatocyte contours and residual nuclei visible at time points where the untreated heat-stroke group had lost nearly all cellular detail.
Skin followed a parallel trajectory. Dermo-epidermal separation, dermal vacuolar degeneration, collagen fragmentation, and nuclear degeneration became increasingly evident beyond 72 hours, appearing earlier or more severely in the heat-stroke group, while the omega-3-pretreated heat-exposed group showed relatively better preservation at matching intervals. By 168 hours, both untreated groups showed complete epidermal-dermal separation, and by 120 hours both heat-exposed groups had reached severe autolysis, although tissue remained histologically identifiable as skin. Crucially, the authors repeatedly flag that these histological observations are qualitative. They explicitly state that the apparent preservation in treated animals does not independently demonstrate that omega-3 slowed postmortem autolysis, and may instead reflect reduced premortem heat-induced injury, meaning the tissue simply started the postmortem period in better condition. Interobserver agreement was also not formally quantified with a statistic such as Cohen’s kappa.
Beyond the treatment question, the study explored whether ALT and AST could serve as quantitative clocks for the postmortem interval. Pearson correlations showed strong positive associations between both enzymes and postmortem interval in all groups, and the team fitted linear and quadratic regression models predicting interval from enzyme levels, validated with nested leave-one-animal-out cross-validation to prevent data leakage. The omega-3-only group achieved the best internal performance, with a cross-validated root mean square error of 5.209 hours and a cross-validated R-squared of 0.906, followed by the heat-stroke group at 5.667 hours and 0.888. ALT was a significant predictor in all groups, while AST reached significance only in the two heat-exposed groups. The authors are careful to label these equations exploratory, internally validated models developed under controlled laboratory conditions that require external validation before any forensic application.
The broader forensic message is that antemortem nutritional and pathological states can leave fingerprints on postmortem measurements, complicating both interval estimation and perimortem injury assessment. The authors propose, as literature-supported hypotheses rather than demonstrated mechanisms, that omega-3’s reported antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, its suppression of NF-kappa-B signaling, and its incorporation into cell and mitochondrial membranes may explain the attenuated findings, but oxidative-stress markers, inflammatory mediators, and molecular pathways were not measured in this study. They also acknowledge the limits of the rat model, the small sample size, and the gap between controlled chamber conditions and the variability of real forensic casework. Larger studies with quantitative histological scoring, mechanistic biomarkers, independent validation cohorts, and human postmortem samples are needed before any of these findings could inform practice. For now, the study stands as a controlled demonstration that what a body experienced before death, and what it was fed beforehand, can measurably reshape the biochemical and histological evidence it leaves behind.

Cyclone Arnab brings rain to Delhi-NCR, air quality to improve
Rain is forecast in Delhi as moisture from Cyclone Arnab interacts with a western disturbance. Here's how the weather could affect air quality.
Delhi is expected to get rain today, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing a yellow alert for the capital.
In its morning update, the weather agency said that very light to light rain, along with thunder and lightning, is likely at a few places in Delhi, prompting a yellow alert to encourage people to stay updated with the situation.
While the rain arrives due to an interaction between multiple factors, the timing of it could help the capital breathe easier than it has in the past days when the air has remained heavy with pollution.
DELHI'S AQI REMAINS HIGH
The showers come just as Delhi is struggling to breathe.
At 9:31 am today, the city's Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 363, according to AQI.in, marking yet another day that had begun with a worrying level of pollution.
The story, worryingly, has been similar in the last few days.
AQI readings between 22 and 28 October swung from around 140 on some afternoons to well above 330 on many nights and mornings.
Just yesterday, on October 28, the AQI was about 367 at 10 am, fell to roughly 125 by late afternoon, and was back above 300 after 10 pm.
The simple reason for the AQI to be moving with the clock is that the daytime Sun helps pollutants rise and spread out, but once it sets, the smog settles back in.
Today might prove to be different.
WILL DELHI'S AQI IMPROVE?
Delhi is expected to get showers, thanks to two weather systems that are working together.
A western disturbance, which travels in from the west, sits over northwest Uttar Pradesh, and Cyclone Arnab, a very severe storm, was expected to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on 28 October.
The forecast of rain and gusty winds offers some hope of temporary relief, but a sustained improvement in Delhi's air quality is not guaranteed.
Rain can wash some airborne particles out of the atmosphere, while stronger winds can disperse pollutants. The extent of the improvement depends on how much rain falls, how long it lasts, wind direction and whether the atmosphere allows pollutants to mix upwards.
The IMD has forecast gusty winds of 30–50 kmph over Delhi on October 29, along with rain and thunderstorms. Rain is also forecast on October 30, before skies turn partly cloudy over the weekend.
The key question is whether the weather will disperse enough pollution to bring down the AQI across the city, rather than producing a brief improvement at a few monitoring stations.
Even if the air clears temporarily, pollution from vehicles, road dust, construction and other sources can build up again. The next few days of AQI readings will show whether the rain and wind have delivered meaningful relief or merely a short-lived respite.
The need for long-term solutions remains even if rain cleans the air for a brief period. What the rain can't do is get rid of the smoke and dust Delhi produces every day.

IMD issued a yellow alert for Delhi-NCR, forecasting rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds, with isolated hailstorms likely in Delhi, Haryana and Chandigarh until 30 October

Moderate rainfall lashed Delhi-NCR on Thursday as the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a yellow alert, warning of continued unsettled weather, thunderstorms and gusty winds. The weather department has also forecast isolated hailstorms in Delhi, Haryana and Chandigarh until 30 October.
The IMD said light to moderate rainfall is likely at several places, accompanied by lightning and strong winds. Wind speeds could reach 40-50 kmph during the morning hours, while gusts of 30-40 kmph are expected during the remainder of the day.
The maximum and minimum temperatures in the national capital are forecast to settle at 27 degrees Celsius and 17 degrees Celsius, respectively, on Thursday.
According to the IMD, cloudy skies and thunderstorms are likely to persist on Friday as the weather system continues to influence Delhi and neighbouring regions. Isolated hailstorms are also possible in parts of Delhi, Haryana and Chandigarh.
Residents have been advised to remain cautious during periods of lightning, hail and strong winds. Gusty conditions could disrupt outdoor activities, while thunderstorms may affect local travel.
The yellow alert signals the need for residents to stay informed about changing weather conditions and follow official advisories.
Despite the rainfall, Delhi's air quality remained in the 'poor' category on Thursday morning. The city's average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 227 at 8 am, according to the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB) All India AQI portal.
PM2.5 and PM10 were identified as the prominent pollutants contributing to the city's pollution levels.
Among the monitoring stations, Uttam Nagar recorded the highest AQI at 340, placing it in the 'very poor' category. Dwarka Sector 8 followed with an AQI of 308, also falling under the 'very poor' classification.
Several other locations reported 'poor' air quality, including CRRI Mathura Road at 299, Punjabi Bagh at 285, Chandni Chowk at 272, Pusa at 271, NSIT Dwarka at 270, Sirifort at 268 and IGI Airport Terminal 3 at 266.
Nangloi recorded an AQI of 260, followed by NSUT Jaffarpur at 253, Alipur at 250, Najafgarh at 243, Mandir Marg at 230, Anand Vihar at 227, Burari Crossing at 226 and CRRI Mathura Road at 299.
In contrast, several areas recorded comparatively better air quality in the 'moderate' category. Burari registered an AQI of 174, Vasundhara Enclave 171, Jharoda Kalan 161, Badarpur 159, Chhawla 154, Ghummanhera 197 and Karala 198.
Under the CPCB's National AQI classification, readings between 101 and 200 fall in the 'moderate' category, while values between 201 and 300 are classified as 'poor'. AQI readings between 301 and 400 fall under the 'very poor' category.
Prolonged exposure to poor air quality can cause breathing discomfort, particularly among people with respiratory conditions. Very poor air quality can increase the risk of respiratory illnesses, especially among children, older adults and those with existing health problems.
With rain and thunderstorms expected to continue across parts of Delhi-NCR, residents will need to monitor both weather alerts and local air quality readings in the coming days.

NTR District Collector G Lakshmisha said rehabilitation centres had been set up in Swarna villages and Swarna wards across the district and all basic amenities were being provided.
He directed officials to ensure uninterrupted supply of food and water, medical assistance and special care for children, senior citizens, women and people with health issues.
The Collector instructed field staff to remain alert and monitor the situation. As part of preventive measures, Town Planning teams visited Amma Kalyanamandapam, Sunnapubatti Centre, Moghalrajpuram, Chittinagar and hill areas on Wednesday and shifted residents from vulnerable houses to rehabilitation centres.
Authorities have also begun identifying and removing unsafe flex boards and hoardings that could pose a threat during strong winds. Meanwhile, under the supervision of the Horticulture Department, 15 special teams comprising 40 personnel have been deployed to identify and trim hazardous tree branches across the city. The teams are using 14 chainsaws and seven JCBs.
Officials said fallen trees and related complaints would be attended to promptly to ensure smooth public and vehicular movement.
